title: Medium exam 7
about: Ten single-choice questions that combine two facts or ask you to trace two or three steps: loops over arguments, escaped dots, startup files, links and permissions, `&&` and `||`, and here-documents.

questions.title: A for loop without a list
questions.text: `loop.sh` contains `for v; do echo "<$v>"; done`. What does `bash loop.sh "a b" c` print?

options.why: With no list, `for` goes over the arguments as they were given, so `a b` stays together.
`for v` with no `in` runs once for each argument of the script.
That is what a single string of all the arguments would give; the loop runs once per argument.

options.t: A syntax error, because `for` needs the word `in` and a list.
options.why: The form without a list is valid and uses the arguments.

questions.title: A literal dot
questions.text: `v` contains the lines `1.5`, `125` and `1x5`. Which command prints only `1.5`?

options.why: The unescaped dot matches any character, so it matches all three lines.
The backslash makes the dot an ordinary character.
`1*` is zero or more ones, so any line containing a `5` matches: all three.
It looks for one or more ones followed by a 5, like `15` or `115`; none of the lines has that.

questions.title: Editing .bashrc
questions.text: You add the line `alias ll='ls -l'` to `~/.bashrc` and, in the terminal you already had open, type `ll`. What happens?

options.t: It works at once, because bash re-reads `.bashrc` before each command.
options.why: `.bashrc` is read when the shell starts.

options.t: `ll` is not found in that terminal; it will work in a new terminal, or after `source ~/.bashrc`.
options.why: The alias is created when the file is read, which happened before you edited it.

options.t: The alias works in every terminal, including this one, but only after a reboot.
options.why: A new shell is enough; no reboot is needed.

options.t: bash gives an error, because aliases cannot be written in `.bashrc`.
options.why: `.bashrc` is precisely the place for the aliases and variables that customise bash.

questions.title: Permissions of a symbolic link
questions.text: Which statement about a symbolic link and permissions is FALSE?

options.t: `ls -l` shows the link itself with the mode `lrwxrwxrwx`.
options.why: True: all its bits are on.

options.t: What you can do through the link is decided by the permissions of the file it points to.
options.why: True: the link does not grant or deny anything by itself.

options.t: `chmod 600 link` changes the mode of the target, not of the link.
options.why: True: `chmod` follows the link.

options.t: Because the link shows `rwxrwxrwx`, anybody can read a target whose mode is `rw-------`.
options.why: False: the target's permissions apply, so only its owner can read it.

questions.title: Header of a script
questions.text: A script must start by printing the name of the machine, the directory it is running in and how many arguments it received. Which line does it?

options.why: The words are printed as plain text; nothing is executed.
Single quotes block the substitutions and the variable, so the text is printed as it is.
The substitution runs `hostname`, `PWD` holds the current directory and `$#` is the number of arguments.
`$hostname` and `$pwd` are variables that do not exist, so only the argument count appears.

questions.title: Init systems
questions.text: Which statement about the initial process and its styles is FALSE?

options.t: System V init was the standard on Linux for many years.
options.why: True: it was also used by other Unix systems such as AIX and Solaris.

options.t: systemd is the initial process on current Ubuntu, Fedora and Debian.
options.why: True.

options.t: systemd can start services in parallel and restart a service that has died.
options.why: True: it handles the dependencies and watches the services.

options.t: launchd is the initial process of Ubuntu and Fedora.
options.why: False: launchd is the one of macOS.

questions.title: Size of a directory
questions.text: Which command prints one single line with the total disk space used by the directory `projects` and everything in it, in a human-readable unit?

options.why: It prints one line per subdirectory, not only the total.
It reports the free and used space of the filesystem that contains the directory.
`-s` gives only the total and `-h` uses units such as K, M and G.
It lists the files with their individual sizes; it does not add them up.

questions.title: Status as a condition
questions.text:
`/nope` does not exist and `/etc` does. What does this print?
```
if ls /nope 2> /dev/null; then echo A; else echo B; fi
if ls /etc > /dev/null; then echo C; else echo D; fi
```

options.why: Hiding the message does not change the status: `ls /nope` still fails, so the `else` branch runs.
`ls /etc` succeeds even though its output goes to `/dev/null`.
`if` looks at the exit status: non-zero for `ls /nope` (so `else`) and zero for `ls /etc` (so `then`).
Both branches are the opposite of what happens: status 0 is "true" for `if`, and any other value is "false".

questions.title: A chain of filters
questions.text:
What does this print?
```
printf 'b,2\na,1\nc,3\n' | sort | head -n 2 | cut -d, -f2
```

options.why: `sort` runs first, so the order starts with `a`.
`head -n 2` keeps only two lines.
After `sort` the lines are `a,1`, `b,2` and `c,3`; `head` keeps the first two and `cut` prints their second field.
`-f2` selects the second field, the number.

questions.title: Here-documents
questions.text:
What does this print?
```
n=4
cat <<EOF
n is $n
EOF
cat <<'EOF'
n is $n
EOF
wc -w <<< "a b c"
```

options.why: With the delimiter quoted (`'EOF'`) the text is taken literally and `$n` is not expanded.
With an unquoted delimiter the shell expands `$n` in the text.
`<<<` gives `wc` the string `a b c`, which has three words.
Unquoted `EOF` expands the variable, quoted `'EOF'` does not, and the here-string has three words.
